en: The Great Ocean of the Nectar of Kṛṣṇa: Oṃ.
He who, when worshipped, remembered, meditated upon, glorified, praised, or heard, bestows immortality—may that Keśava protect me. // MKm 1 //
I shall describe this great ocean of the nectar Kṛṣṇa for the sake of pacifying this entire world, which is tormented by the threefold suffering.
Those men are mere cattle in this world; what fruit is there in their living, by whom the initiation of Hari has not been received or Janārdana has not been worshipped?
In this most terrible saṃsāra, which is agitated by the fear of birth and disease, this one alone is honored as the highly fortunate Adhokṣaja. // MKm_4 //
He indeed is a man of merit in this world, for by him his lineage is adorned— he by whom Viṣṇu has been propitiated, the support of all living beings.
Among sacrifices, austerities, and indeed all auspicious deeds,
the constant worship of Hari always yields the most distinguished fruit for human beings.
Those men who constantly worship Hari, the destroyer of all sins and the eradicator of the impurities of the Kali age, are themselves worthy of veneration just as Hari is.
O Sage, there is nothing that brings greater benefit to men than the propitiation of Viṣṇu;
yet in this dark age, he is constantly worshipped by men in this world.
When the Lord of all gods, who bears the conch, discus, and mace, is worshipped,
all the gods are worshipped, because Hari is omnipresent.
A man who takes refuge in Keśava— the well-worshipped Lord of all worlds, honored by gods and asuras, the slayer of Kaṃsa and the enemy of Keśin— does not go to hell.
By worshipping Govinda even once with a *bilva* leaf,
a person becomes a partaker of liberation, free from all affliction, and shall dwell for a long time in the world of Viṣṇu.
He by whom [the Buddha] has been worshipped even once, or saluted even with contempt, goes to the supreme state which is difficult even for the gods to attain. // MKm 12 //
Nārada said:
The worship of the Lord Viṣṇu himself— the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the God of gods, and the protector of all worlds— is the true fruit of birth.
Pulastya said:
Worshipped with devotion by men using *dūrvā* sprouts, Hari, the Supreme Person, indeed bestows that fruit which is difficult to obtain even through all sacrifices.
O Lord of the gods, Hari, the wielder of the conch and discus, when worshipped even with water alone according to the prescribed rite, bestows his fruit which is easily attained.
Being cooked in hell and rebuked by Yama, he was asked:
"Why was the god Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, not worshipped by you?"
Dharma said:
"Has he not been worshipped by you— that Narasiṃha, Hṛṣīkeśa, whose eyes resemble lotuses, who grants liberation to men through mere remembrance?"
But even in the absence of material offerings, he who, being honored even with water alone,
grants his own abode— has he not been honored by you?
Even those who have remained in the womb or have died are robbed and utterly ruined if they have not obtained initiation into Hari, which liberates one from all suffering. // MKm 19 //
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
By whomsoever the God of gods, Janārdana, has been worshipped even once, by him all that is to be done has been accomplished, and he has attained the supreme state.
O Lord of Gods, I speak the truth: there exists no other means for attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa than the worship of Hṛṣīkeśa. // MKm_21 //
Salutations again and again even to those who offer obeisance to that Viṣṇu, the Sacrificial Boar of immeasurable splendor. // MKm_22 //
Marīci said:
"O Prince, that supreme station is not attained by men who have failed to propitiate Govinda; therefore, worship Acyuta."
Atri:
That person for whom Janārdana is satisfied is the highest of the high;
he attains the imperishable state—this truth has been spoken by me.
Aṅgiras said:
Worship Govinda, within whom all this very world exists as the self designated by the name "the Unfallen," if you desire that supreme state. (MKm 25)
Pulaha: By propitiating Hari— who is the supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, and that which is the eternal Brahman— one attains even liberation, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain.
Indra attained the supreme station of Indra by propitiating Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Universe and the Lord of Sacrifice; therefore, O observer of noble vows, propitiate Him.
When Viṣṇu is propitiated by the mind, one obtains whatever one desires, even a station within the three worlds— how much more so those that are increasingly transcendent?
Those who always remember Viṣṇu, the wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace,
being completely liberated from all sins, they enter the Supreme Brahman.
Then [he worships] Aniruddha, the Lord of Gods, and after that Pradyumna;
then the god Saṃkarṣaṇa, and Vāsudeva, who is higher than the highest.
"There is nothing superior to Vāsudeva"—this is the certainty of the Vedānta;
for those who have entered into Vāsudeva, how could there be any returning again?
Ātreya said:
Whatever desires a man or a woman of excellent complexion may wish for, he or she attains those abundant rewards by propitiating Janārdana.
Pulaha said: "O Brahmā,
what man on earth would wish to cross the ocean with his two arms?"
Who, without having propitiated Vāsudeva, desires to go to liberation?
Śaṃkara said:
For that man in whom remorse arises after a sin has been committed,
the supreme expiation prescribed for him is the remembrance of Hari.
For indeed, in this world, devotion toward Govinda, as well as remembrance and glorification, does not arise in those who lack merit, who are deluded, and whose natures are crooked.
At that very moment, a person is liberated from birth, suffering, old age, and the like— once they have conquered the senses and purified the self, whenever they remember Hari.
When the terrible Kali age has arrived, devoid of righteousness and knowledge, no one will remember the god Kṛṣṇa, who removes the impurities of the Kali age.
In the Kali age, the deluded mortal does not perform the remembrance or the chanting of Hari, the God of gods, who removes the suffering of birth.
Those who always remember Viṣṇu with a pure inner self, having abandoned worldly existence, go to the stainless realm of Viṣṇu.
A person who constantly recollects Vāsudeva is never afflicted by the bonds of saṃsāra— the sufferings of conception, birth, old age, and disease.
Whoever should remember the one whose banner is Garuḍa would not see the most terrible path of Yama, nor the hells, nor Yama himself, even in a dream.
He who has the form of Hari in his heart, His name in his mouth, the food offering in his stomach,
and the water from His feet and the remains of His garland upon his head— that person is Acyuta himself.
The remembrance of Govinda quickly burns away the great mountain of a person's mass of sins, just as fire consumes a heap of cotton without a doubt.
Agastya said:
By the mere remembrance of Kṛṣṇa, the cage of the multitude of sins shatters into a hundred pieces, just as a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
Those who are devoted to Kṛṣṇa, who remember Kṛṣṇa, who are permeated by Him, and whose minds are fixed on Him— they,
upon the dissolution of the body, enter Viṣṇu, just as an oblation consecrated with mantras enters the fire.
That is a loss, that is a great defect, and that is blindness, stupidity, and muteness,
if for even a moment or an instant Vāsudeva is not meditated upon.
The man named Nārāyaṇa is declared on earth to be the thief who completely subdues men;
by his mere remembrance, he burns away the entire accumulation of sins gathered over many lifetimes without exception.
By the mere recollection of Vāsudeva, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
the sin accumulated over ten million lifetimes perishes at that very moment.
What need has he for many sacred fords, what need for austerities, or what need for sacrifices—
he who constantly meditates upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa with undivided mind?
Those men who, free from passion and knowing the higher and the lower, constantly remember Nārāyaṇa, the teacher of the gods,
with such meditation that their minds are cleansed of defilement— they do not drink the milk from a mother’s breast again.
Therefore, O mind, contemplate Vāsudeva here day and night;
for he, when meditated upon by men, surely destroys the bondage of saṃsāra.
Having churned all the scriptures and reflected upon them again and again, this one thing is well-established: Nārāyaṇa is to be meditated upon at all times.
I go for refuge to that unborn and eternal Hari, by remembering whom a person becomes a vessel for all auspiciousness.

Whatever merit is prescribed in the Vedas, in sacrifices, in austerities, in gifts, in sacred fords, and in vows— whether in rites performed for one's own sake or for the public good— that merit indeed resides in the remembrance of Vāsudeva.
Aurva said:
By worshipping Viṣṇu alone, a person obtains whatever fruit they desire with their mind— whether it be abundant or even very small— in its entirety and without fail.
O Maitreya, the chanting of the Name with devotion is the unsurpassed dissolution of all sins, just as fire is for [the impurities of] metals.
The most fierce impurity of the Kali age, which brings the suffering of hell to men,
is instantly dissolved when Acyuta is glorified even once.
Those who have taken refuge in Keśava attain liberation without effort;
yet Śakra and the other gods arise as adversaries to obstruct that attainment.
Having reached the four oceans, one finds that nowhere in the most excellent Jambūdvīpa is there any man other than Keśava who can heal all evils.
That fruit which one obtains by worshipping Hari with devotion even for hundreds of years in the Kṛta age, one attains in its entirety in the Kali age simply by chanting the praises of Keśava.
But when Dharma declines upon the arrival of the terrible Kali age, then no one shall proclaim the infallible God who grants liberation.
Even when his name is uttered involuntarily, a person is instantly freed from all sins, just as deer are by lions.
The mantra "Nārāyaṇa" exists, and speech exists that is subject to one's control;
yet that they sink into a terrible hell—this is truly marvelous.
Those who are afflicted, despondent, weakened, and terrified, even when beset by terrible diseases,
become free from suffering and attain happiness simply by chanting the name of Nārāyaṇa.
Kauśika:
Those by whom the name "Kṛṣṇa" has been uttered even once do not enter the womb, nor the house of a mother, nor the unbearable realm of Yama.
Where is the ascent to the vault of heaven, characterized by rebirth, and where is the recitation of "Vāsudeva," the unsurpassed seed of liberation?
Having understood this with your intellect, speak these two syllables, "Ha-ri";
by the mere remembrance of Kṛṣṇa, one is never born again anywhere.
O tongue of mine, devoid of affection, why do you not speak of Hari?
Speak of Hari, O auspicious one; Hari is the boat for the ocean of saṃsāra.
In this truly essence-less cycle of existence, Hari is indeed the most essential of essences;
those devoid of merit do not find Him, just as deer do not find water.
What need has he for Kurukṣetra, or for Kāśī, or for Puṣkara?
The two syllables "Ha-ri" abide at the tip of his tongue.
Brahmā said:
In this truly essence-less cycle of existence, one essence has indeed been determined:
the propitiation of Hari, the Lord of all the worlds, is that essence.
That is a true tongue which praises Hari; that is a true mind which is offered to Him;
those alone are praiseworthy hands which perform His worship.
But he who is eternally devoted to Viṣṇu, possessing firm devotion and having conquered his senses,
goes to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu even while dwelling in his own home.
Śaṅkara said: "Excellent, excellent, O illustrious one! Excellent, O destroyer of the Dānavas, that you, knower of dharma, inquire of me concerning the propitiation of Keśava."
O Bhārgava, for those who have not burned away their sins entirely, devotion to Keśava does not arise even for a moment, half a moment, or even for a muhūrta.
What use is that mind which does not abide in Keśava?
A mind that rests in Him is the purposeful cause for attaining the fruit of liberation.
That which does not praise Hari is not truly a tongue; that by which His deeds have not been heard is not truly an ear. // MKm 77 //
Surely that is a lotus-root in the throat, or perhaps a disease called a "double tongue"; for it is not a tongue which does not speak of the virtues of Hari.
O twice-born one, what purpose is served by these [senses] which have become a burden for that beast of a man?
But those two feet are fruitful, O illustrious one, which go to the abode of Keśava; and those two eyes are fruitful, by which Hari is beheld.
O twice-born one, what need has he for feet that wander in vain, by which a living being does not go to behold the abode of Keśava?
O knower of dharma, even the status of a seer (ṛṣi) among sages who know the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences and whose selves are purified should be understood as arising from his grace.
Upon a couch of variegated jewels, those who possess great enjoyments sport with celestial women; this is the fruit of recollecting Keśava.
One who might perform a thousand times a thousand horse-sacrifices does not obtain that fruit which is attained by those devoted to Him.
O each and every one of you men, why do you not fold your hands in salutation to the Supreme Person?
What effort is required of you who perform religious rites? For the fruit thereof is the state of the Infallible One.
That person who performs a single circumambulation of Viṣṇu’s temple with devotion obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
But he who performs circumambulation endowed with devotion to Hari goes to the world of Viṣṇu by means of a celestial chariot yoked with swans.
Thousands of millions of sacred fords and hundreds of millions of vows do not equal even a sixteenth part of a single prostration to Nārāyaṇa.
With the chest, the head, the gaze, the mind, as well as the speech,
the two feet, the two hands, and the two knees— the prostration with eight limbs is thus proclaimed.
Even for one who performs a prostration to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow with deceit, the sin accumulated over hundreds of births is surely destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
For those foremost men who are in the ocean of saṃsāra and have committed evil deeds,
there is no other supporter except for Nārāyaṇa, the supreme Lord of the World.
O Bhārata, for as many thousands of years as there are particles of dust on his body when it is covered with dust, he is honored in the world of Viṣṇu.
The food offered to Viṣṇu is purifying and is declared by the sages to be excellent nourishment;
having eaten the food offering of another deity, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
The fruit that is obtained by men from eating the food offering (naivedya) of Viṣṇu cannot be attained even by thousands of millions of lunar fasts nor by tens of millions of month-long fasts.
Rivers that do not flow to the ocean yield their fruit after three nights;
those that flow to the ocean, however, do so after a fortnight, and the lord of rivers (the ocean) after a month.
The gift of a cow yields fruit for six months, while the Ganges yields it for a year;
yet these do not equal even a sixteenth part of the water from Viṣṇu’s feet.

The Gaṅgā, Prayāga, Gayā, Puṣkara, Naimiṣa, and the Kurujāṅgala regions—these waters of sacred fords (tīrtha) purify sin only after being resorted to many times over a long period; but the water from the feet of the Blessed One purifies it immediately.
Whatever sacred fords exist within the cosmic egg,
they are not worth even a sixteenth part of the water from Viṣṇu’s feet.
Drinking the water used for washing Viṣṇu’s feet as a bath and holding it upon one's head,
one is liberated from all sins and shall attain the perfection of Vaiṣṇava.

Just as the water used for washing the feet, the remains of the garland, the ointment, the food offering, the remnants of the incense, and the light-offering of Hari are meritorious, so too [is the worship of his devotees].
The consumption of the Tulasī pollen and the food offering (naivedya),
as well as wearing the remains of the offering (nirmālya) upon the head, destroys even the greatest of sins.
Whether with devotion or without devotion, the sight or even the touch of a stone marked with the discus destroys all sins.
The deity born from the Śālagrāma stone and the deity born from Dvāravatī—
by the water used for bathing both of them, one removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
O Vasundharā, wherever one marked with the discus resides— even in a barbarian land or an impure place— that area for three yojanas is my own field.
The deity born from Śālagrāma, the stone adorned with the marks of the discus—
wherever it is carried, there it is superior to a hundred elephants.
The Lord originates from Śālagrāma; the Lord originates from Dvāravatī.
Where there is a union of both, there is liberation—of this there is no doubt.
Since Hari grants liberation here from all places of liberation, what need has he who possesses [him] in all states of being for those [places]?
"Hari goes, Hari goes!"— even he who speaks thus under the pretext of being a bandit attains a good rebirth, just like those of meritorious deeds.
He who, abandoning Vāsudeva, worships another deity—
that deluded soul abandons the nectar of immortality and consumes the hālāhala poison.
Just as some man might drink another beverage after having abandoned the nectar of immortality,
so too do they worship another deity after having forsaken Hari.
Just as one might abandon one's own duty (svadharma) and practice the duty of another (paradharma),
so too do they abandon Hari and worship another deity.
Just as one who is deluded in mind might abandon a cow and pay homage to a donkey,
so too do they abandon Hari and worship another deity.
He who, abandoning Vāsudeva, worships another deity, is like a foolish man who, while thirsty on the banks of the Ganges, digs a well.
Just as a person might abandon the water of the Ganges to drink from a well,
so too is he who, having forsaken Hari, worships another deity.
Just as one who abandons his own mother might instead pay homage to a dog-cooker (śvapākī),
so too is he who, having abandoned Hari, worships another deity.
As long as this body is healthy, free from disease, and endowed with its faculties, so long perform what is beneficial for yourself; later, you will be tormented by regret.
As long as there is health in the body and proficiency in the sense organs, so long worship Govinda; make your life meaningful.
Let Hṛṣīkeśa be remembered; for who remembers Hṛṣīkeśa when the senses are firm, and who remembers Hṛṣīkeśa when the senses are not firm?
As long as a living being contemplates sense objects that are like poison, so long will they suffer;
but if one remembers Viṣṇu, who would not be liberated from bondage?
As long as a living being prattles on about sense-objects which are like poison,
if he remembers Viṣṇu during that time, who would not be liberated from bondage?
Sūta said:
Having correctly ascertained the lunar day (tithi) as proclaimed by astrologers, O brahmins, the fast must be observed; otherwise, one shall go to hell.
Whether at the waning or the waxing [of the moon], or when the end of the day arrives, one should observe the meritorious Dvādaśī; one should abandon that which is overlapped by the previous day.
A man who observes a day of the lunar month as joined with the previous one cuts away his own merits,
leading to the destruction of his lineage and the loss of his prosperity.
O best of Brahmins, when there is a *kalā* overlap, one should abandon the eleventh day for the sake of the tenth;
one should discard it just as one would Gaṅgā water touched by a drop of liquor.

O best of the twice-born, during the dog-days one should consume the five products of the cow; on the tenth day, one should abandon a woman who has been defiled, and likewise on the eleventh day of both fortnights.
Therefore, O Brahmins, Ekādaśī should never be observed as pierced;
for a pierced day destroys former merit, just as the husband of a Śūdra woman destroys the merit of a Śrāddha rite.
Whatever has been chanted, given, offered in sacrifice, bathed, or likewise whatever worship was performed for Hari—
all that goes to destruction, just as darkness does at the rising of the sun.
O Brahmin, when the Ekādaśī coincides with a *dinakṣaya* (the loss of a lunar day),
one should fast on the Dvādaśī and perform the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) on the Trayodaśī.
All [fasting days], beginning with the *pratipad*, are to be understood as complete from sunrise until sunrise, with the exception of the day of Hari (the eleventh lunar day).
If the tenth lunar day is seen at the time of sunrise,
then the fasting on the eleventh day should be known as the root of sin.
If the tenth day is seen at the time of sunrise,
the eleventh day should not be observed there, for it destroys virtue, desire, and wealth.
The four *ghaṭikās* of morning are called the dawn;
this is known as the time for bathing for ascetics, equal to the waters of the Gaṅgā.
O Brahmins, when [the Ekādaśī] is joined with two muhūrtas before sunrise,
it is called "Sampūrṇaikādaśī," and the observer of the vow should fast on that very day.
When Ekādaśī extends for three ghaṭikās prior to sunrise, it is called "doubtful Ekādaśī" (sandigdhaikādaśī); it must be avoided, as it destroys merit and wealth.
For the sake of increasing one's sons and grandsons, one should observe a fast on the twelfth day;
the merit therein is equal to a hundred sacrifices, and the breaking of the fast should take place on the thirteenth day.
When Ekādaśī extends for two ghaṭikās prior to sunrise,
it is called "mixed" (saṅkīrṇa) Ekādaśī and should be avoided by those desiring merit, wealth, and [other worldly goals].
For the sake of increasing the kingdom for one's son, there should be a fast on the twelfth day;
therein lies the merit of a hundred sacrifices, and the breaking of the fast should take place on the thirteenth day.
If the Gāndhārī fast is observed on a day joined with the remainder of the tenth lunar day, her hundred sons were lost; therefore, one should avoid it.
When there are conflicting scriptural authorities among the Brāhmaṇas who dispute one another,
the meritorious Dvādaśī should be observed as a fast, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should be performed on the Trayodaśī.
When the eleventh day is pierced [by the preceding lunar day] and the Śravaṇa asterism likewise occurs,
the meritorious twelfth day should be observed as a fast on both fortnights.
Thousands of solar eclipses and tens of thousands of Vyatīpāta yogas, even a hundred thousand new moon days, are not worth a sixteenth part of the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī).
Even if pure, the twelfth day (dvādaśī) should be accepted if there is a twelfth day following it;
for the tenth day (daśamī) is known as poison, while the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) is nectar.
That [eleventh day] which has poison as its primary part should be avoided, but that which is primarily nectar should be accepted.
He who, out of dull-wittedness, should partake of food on the twelfth day or observe the fast for Hari on a pierced [tithi], goes to hell.

Whatever other statements there may be concerning the worship of pierced [objects], or those devoted to the worship of Dhanada (Kubera), they do not amount to even a ten-thousandth part of the Vaiṣṇava state.
Alternatively, for the purpose of deluding [the world], Lord Hari Janārdana, having been requested by Mohinī, assumed the form of Vyāsa and caused [the work] to be composed.
For the sake of increasing the worship of the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada) and for the accumulation of great riches;
for the purpose of deluding the Asuras and for the proliferation of heretics;
and likewise for the failure to recognize one's own true nature and for the non-attainment of that true nature. // MKm 145 //

Having thus abandoned one who has been pierced [by the arrow], by fasting on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), the sin accumulated over ten million lifetimes is destroyed by that single act alone; even more than ten million times greater is the merit for one who avoids what is forbidden by other people.
Whatever sin has been committed since beginningless time, and whatever one will commit hereafter— all that goes to destruction through the fasting of others;
nor is anyone dearer to Keśava than they, nor even to me.
Indeed, when the eleventh day (ekādaśī) is not pierced [by the twelfth], one should not abandon the twelfth day;
for both the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) and death, the lunar day is considered to be that which exists at the actual moment.
Whether he be a celibate student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or likewise an ascetic;
whether he be a Brahmin, a Kshatriya, a Vaishya, or a Shudra; or likewise a woman who has a husband.
Likewise, those who are widowed, as well as others such as chariot-makers and weavers,
should not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight.
But he whose consciousness is shrouded by delusion and eats on the eleventh day, whether it be the bright or the dark fortnight, certainly goes to hell.
He who, out of delusion, discriminates between Ekādaśī as "white" or "black," being a doer of evil, surely goes to hell; there is no doubt about this.
Just as a cow— whether white or black— must never be killed, O beautiful lady,
one should not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight.

Whatever statements there may be regarding the avoidance of Ekādaśī on a Kṛṣṇa day, as well as the prohibition of Bharaṇī and other such asterisms, they apply only to those who seek specific desired fruits.
For even those possessed of desire should indeed observe the fast for the sake of the eternal goal,
always for the purpose of pleasing Hari, and not out of regard for sensual pleasure.

Therefore, for the sake of preventing transgression, for the purpose of pleasing Hari, or for the attainment of the world of Viṣṇu, one should always observe a fast on the Śukla (bright) or Kṛṣṇa (dark) [fortnight] when it is joined with the asterism Bharaṇī and so forth.
If another twelfth day occurs, even by a mere *kalā* or a *ghaṭikā*,
it destroys all twelve twelfth days if the breaking of the fast is performed on the preceding day.
If the twelfth day (dvādaśī) is exceeded, one should not fast on it;
for by doing so, one destroys twelve future dvādaśīs, and the twelfth day itself is thus transgressed.
He who eats on the preceding day when the twelfth lunar day is an extra day (atiriktā) destroys twelve twelfth days; therefore, one should not abandon the twelfth day.
The merit accumulated over five years is destroyed for that person of very dull intellect who does not fast on the twelfth lunar day conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism.
Having fasted on the eleventh day, one may then fast on the twelfth as well; there shall be no lapse of the rule, for Hari is the deity of both.
Even if one breaks the fast with water alone, one does not incur any fault;
for the wise have declared that water is both "eaten" and "uneaten.
Therefore, I shall perform the conclusion of my vow with water alone.
Neither Kāśī, nor Gayā, nor the Gaṅgā, nor the Revā, nor the Gautamī,
nor even the field of the Kauravas, O King, is equal to a single day of Hari.
Thousands of horse sacrifices and tens of thousands of Vājapeya sacrifices are not worth even a sixteenth part of the fast of Ekādaśī.
O King of kings, by the fire arising from Ekādaśī, even the fuel of sin produced over a hundred lifetimes is reduced to ashes.
There exists nothing on earth for men so purifying as this day of Padmanābha, which destroys all transgressions.
O lord of men, sins remain within this body for as long as a living being does not observe the auspicious fast on the day of Padmanābha.
O Lord, whatever sin has been committed through the eleven sense organs,
one may bring all of that to dissolution by fasting on the eleventh day.
O King, there exists no protection against sin equal to Ekādaśī; even when observed under a pretext, it does not reveal the Sun (the day of the new moon).
Śrī Vedavyāsa said:
He who eats on the eleventh day of both fortnights is a killer of a Brahmin, a killer of a cow, a thief, and one who violates the teacher’s bed.
Better is sexual intercourse with one's own mother, better is the eating of cow-flesh,
better is the killing of a Brahmin or the drinking of liquor than eating on the eleventh day.
On the meritorious day of Ekādaśī, those who eat are the lowest of men; having looked upon their faces, one should look at the sun.
Whatever sins exist on earth, such as the killing of a Brahmin and others,
abide taking refuge in food when the day of Hari has arrived.
Rugmāṅgada said:
That sinful man who, being more than eight years old but not yet reaching eighty, eats when the day of Viṣṇu has arrived. // MKm_174 //
Whether it be a father, a son, a wife, or even a friend,
whoever eats on the day of Padmanābha should be restrained like a thief.
Dharmavibhūṣaṇa said:
"On the day of Hari, O people, you should remain standing in the morning, eating only one meal, all of you abstaining from pungent and salty foods and consuming only sacrificial food (haviṣya)."
Sleeping on the bare ground and deprived of the company of your beloveds,
remember the Lord of the gods, the ancient Supreme Person.
For you shall observe the fast while consuming only a single meal,
having not yet performed the accumulation of funeral offerings, nor the rites of water-sprinkling and rice-balls.
Brahmā said:
Having observed the meritorious twelfth day (dvādaśī), which bestows the destruction of all evils,
one sees neither Yama, nor the hells, nor any torment.
"O fair-faced one, the ancient scriptures proclaim again and again here:
'One must not eat, one must not eat when the day of Hari has arrived.'"
The twelfth day (dvādaśī) must not be neglected as long as one’s life continues;
Hṛṣīkeśa is to be worshipped with a pure inner self.
O Brahmins, Hṛṣīkeśa is to be grasped through devotion, not by means of wealth;
Viṣṇu, when worshipped with devotion, bestows the desired fruit.
Even when worshipped with water alone, the Lord of the World, the destroyer of afflictions,
quickly attains satisfaction, just as those afflicted by thirst are satisfied by water.
Whether I am sitting, lying down, standing, or even walking,
O Lotus-eyed One, take delight always within my heart.
O all-pervading one, the soul of all, who never wavers in any state— rejoice, O lotus-eyed Nṛsiṃha, within my heart!
O lotus-eyed Śrī Kṛṣṇa, grant me your hand’s support at all times as I sink into this terrible ocean of worldly existence.
Save me, save me, O Lord of the World! O Vāsudeva, Acyuta, Immutable One! Lift me up, O Govinda, from this ocean of suffering and saṃsāra.
This supreme merit is a secret, purifying, and destroyer of evil;
it bestows long life and fame, and destroys the misfortunes and bad dreams of the Kali age.
In the Kali age, however great the sin arising from killing, theft, and so forth may be,
when Govinda is remembered in the mind, it is consumed like a heap of cotton.
In the Kali age, for those devoted to Keśava, no fear exists anywhere;
when He is remembered, glorified, or meditated upon, sin goes to its destruction.
This treatise should be studied and listened to without malice;
it should be given again and again to those who are devoted and righteous.
One who studies this scripture, which contains the supreme majesty of Viṣṇu,
becomes completely liberated from all sins and attains the highest state.
Having heard the Dharma, one understands; having heard it, one abandons wrong-mindedness;
having heard it, one attains knowledge; and having heard it, one goes to liberation.
Therefore, this should indeed always be proclaimed and heard;
however, it must never under any circumstances be given to those consumed by the forest fire of fallacious reasoning.
For those living beings on earth who have died from drinking the poison of saṃsāra, Kṛṣṇa is remembered as a great ocean of nectar for their immortality.
He whose body is constantly moistened by the water used for washing the feet is,
in effect, bathed every day by thousands of millions of sacred fords.
What is the use of resorting to thousands of millions of sacred fords,
if one were to drink daily the water that has fallen from the Śālagrāma stone?
The gods, including Indra, desire the touch of the hands of those who perform the touching of a *śālagrāma* stone day after day.
The fire of hell is unbearable, as are the servants of Yama; the path of the Lord of Death is treacherous, and the state of a preta is exceedingly dreadful.
Reflecting thus even with the mind, one should turn away from sin;
one should never abandon the remembrance and glorification of Viṣṇu.

By whomsoever the two syllables "Ha-ri" have been uttered even once,
the girdle has been fastened by him for the journey toward liberation.
In this way, the gods beginning with Brahmā and the sages whose wealth is austerity glorify the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the foremost of the gods.
Of what use are gifts to him, of what use are sacred fords, of what use are austerities, or of what use are sacrifices,
for one who constantly meditates upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa with undivided mind?
For those in whose hearts dwells the Blessed Lord Hari, the abode of auspiciousness, there is perpetual festival, eternal constancy, everlasting splendor, and constant victory.
Living beyond fourteen years, a person— whether male or female— will inevitably acquire a human body that is no less than ten years old.
The fourteen [realms] exist above, and saṃsāra is without beginning; therefore, O Great Sage, what hope for liberation can there be without knowing the supreme deity?
Until the fourteenth year, however, this [person] regularly performs the actions that serve as the causes for ten future bodies;
therefore, how could liberation ever occur through the exhaustion of karma?
If equal honor is shown to those who are unequal, or likewise equal honor to those who are unequal,
then even a god will surely fall from his own station.
Wealth, kinship, age, ritual action, and learning as the fifth—these are the grounds for respect; each subsequent one is more weighty than the preceding.
Viṣṇu is pleased with that man who offers worship according to merit and maintains an impartial view toward all living beings.
One who performs acts of honor and so forth toward friends, fathers, enemies, and sons in the same manner as one would toward oneself is said to possess equanimous mind.
One should not apply the horizontal sectarian mark (tiryakpuṇḍra), even when death has arrived;
nor should one utter any name other than the supreme Nārāyaṇa.
Whoever eats the remains of the deity’s food offering day after day,
for every grain of rice, he shall obtain merit exceeding that of a hundred Cāndrāyaṇa fasts.
One on whose forehead a straight, gentle vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) is seen—even if he is a Caṇḍāla—is a pure soul and certainly worthy of worship; of this there is no doubt.
Even a person who is impure, lacking in proper conduct, or committing evil with the mind,
shall always remain pure if he is marked with the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*.
Having beheld the faces of those who are devoid of the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), which resemble a cremation ground, one should look at the sun.
Sacrifice, charity, austerity, Vedic study, and the libations to the ancestors—
all these become fruitless if performed without the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*.
Whomever one whose limbs are smeared with *gopīcandana* beholds with the eye, that person one should know to be pure; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
The ancestors clap their hands and the grandfathers dance, saying:
"A devotee of Viṣṇu has been born in our family; he will deliver us."
The life of one devoted to Viṣṇu, even for five days,
is superior to that of one devoid of devotion to Keśava, even for thousands of kalpas.
Of what use is he who is born merely as a burden to the earth, a veritable enemy of food,

Whoever gives sandalwood ground by cowherds, even if only the size of a mustard seed, to the twice-born, purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation.
The wise person should always perform actions that have been prescribed, yet should remain perpetually free from desire.
One who possesses knowledge of the past and the future and is capable of uprooting the three worlds—
even such a person should not abandon the conduct prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti.
Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (upaniṣad),
that alone becomes more powerful.
"Performing actions here in this world, one should desire to live for a hundred years;
thus it is for you, and not otherwise than this—for action does not cling to a person."
The conduct of the virtuous and the satisfaction of one's own self are [authoritative]; for dharma is that which is ordained by the Vedas, while adharma is its opposite.
But that which is performed without desire and preceded by knowledge is called "withdrawn" (nivṛtta) here; indeed, one who practices what is withdrawn attains the eternal Brahman.
